log_node_02: Intermediate narration (also called layered chronological sequencing) tracks events when a text uses more than one kind of time marker at once. Authors mix exact dates, relative phrases and order words, so you must combine them to rebuild the real timeline. Recognizing how these markers work together stops you from placing an event too early or too late, which is the most common sequencing mistake. Watch for anchors such as 'in 1998' or 'on Monday', gap markers such as 'two days later', 'soon after' and 'within a week', and order words like 'next' and 'afterward'. For instance, in 'On Monday the team tested the engine; two days later it failed; soon after, engineers found a cracked valve,' the day anchors the story and each gap marker counts forward from the event before it.
log_node_03: Advanced narration (sometimes called non-linear chronology) appears when the order of telling differs from the order of events. Authors use flashbacks, flash-forwards and overlapping storylines to build suspense or explain causes, so the first event you read is not always the first that happened. Recognizing this lets you rebuild the true timeline and answer questions about what led to what. Key markers include past-perfect verbs such as 'had already' and 'had been', backward pointers such as 'earlier', 'years before' and 'by the time', and overlap words such as 'meanwhile' and 'at the same moment'. For instance, 'By the time the rescue boat arrived, the crew had spent two nights on the reef' mentions the arrival first, yet the verb 'had spent' shows the nights on the reef happened earlier.
log_node_04: A definition pattern (also called a definition-and-classification structure) explains what a term means by naming it, placing it in a larger group, and stating what makes it different from other members of that group. Authors use it in textbooks and reports whenever they introduce a key idea the reader must understand before going further. Recognizing the pattern helps you find the exact meaning quickly and see which details are essential and which are extra. Key signal phrases include 'is defined as', 'refers to', 'means', 'is a type of' and 'is known as'. For instance, in 'A volcano is a type of mountain that forms when molten rock erupts through the Earth's crust,' the term comes first, 'a type of mountain' gives its group, and the rest tells you what sets it apart.
log_node_05: A multi-part definition (sometimes called an extended definition) goes beyond one sentence: after naming the term and its group, the author adds several characteristics, each one sharpening the full picture. Writers use this structure for complex ideas that a single line cannot capture, often spreading the parts across a whole paragraph. Recognizing it helps you collect every characteristic instead of stopping at the first, which matters when a question asks for a complete meaning. Watch for 'is characterized by', 'one feature is', 'another feature', 'in addition' and 'also'. For instance, a passage might define a rainforest as a dense forest, then add that it receives heavy rain all year, then note that it holds more plant species than any other land habitat; each added feature narrows the meaning further.
log_node_06: A full academic definition (also called a formal or expanded definition) combines the term, its category, its distinguishing features and concrete examples, often with a restatement for extra clarity. Scholars use it to set exact boundaries around a concept so readers apply it correctly in an argument. Recognizing each part helps you separate the definition itself from its illustrations and notice when a writer narrows or widens the meaning. Key markers include 'is formally defined as', 'falls under', 'in other words', 'that is', 'for example' and 'a case in point'. For instance, an economics text might define inflation as a sustained rise in general prices, restate it as money losing buying power, and then give the example of bread costing more each year; the example only makes sense once the definition is clear.
log_node_07: A comparison-and-contrast pattern (often called a compare-contrast structure) shows how two subjects are alike and how they differ. Authors use it to help readers judge between options, understand a new idea through a familiar one, or see what makes each subject unique. Recognizing it helps you sort details into two columns, similarities and differences, so you never mix up which fact belongs to which subject. Key similarity signals include 'similarly', 'likewise', 'both' and 'just as', while difference signals include 'however', 'in contrast', 'whereas' and 'unlike'. For instance, 'Both cats and dogs make loyal pets; however, cats usually need less outdoor exercise' uses 'both' to show a shared trait and 'however' to switch to a difference between the two animals.
log_node_08: A four-part comparison (also known as a structured compare-contrast essay) moves through a clear plan: it introduces two subjects, explains their similarities, explains their differences, and ends with a judgment that weighs them together. Writers use this order so readers can follow a balanced argument before reaching a conclusion. Recognizing the four parts helps you predict where each paragraph belongs and find the writer's final verdict quickly. Watch for opening sentences that name both subjects, similarity markers like 'both' and 'in the same way', turning points like 'on the other hand', and closing signals like 'overall' or 'taken together'. For instance, an essay on trains and buses might open with both, note that each reduces traffic, contrast their costs, and end with 'Overall, trains suit long routes better'; that last sentence is the verdict.
log_node_09: A multi-criteria comparison (sometimes called a point-by-point analysis) judges two or more subjects against several separate standards, such as cost, speed and safety, one criterion at a time. Academic writers use it when a simple better-or-worse answer would hide important trade-offs. Recognizing it helps you track which subject wins on each criterion, so you can explain a conclusion that is mixed rather than one-sided. Key markers include criterion phrases like 'in terms of', 'with regard to' and 'when it comes to', and pivot words such as 'whereas', 'conversely' and 'yet'. For instance, a report might say electric cars cost more to buy, yet cost less to run, whereas petrol cars refuel faster; each clause tests a different criterion, so neither car simply wins.
log_node_10: A cause-and-effect pattern (also called a causal structure) explains why something happened and what happened because of it. Authors use it in science, history and news writing to connect events instead of just listing them. Recognizing it helps you answer why questions and see how one change leads to another. Cause signals include 'because', 'since' and 'due to', while effect signals include 'as a result', 'therefore', 'so' and 'consequently'. Remember that the cause always happens before its effect, even when the sentence mentions the effect first. For instance, in 'The bridge closed because floodwater damaged its supports,' the word 'because' shows that the damaged supports came first and caused the closure, even though the closure is named first.
log_node_11: A chained cause-and-effect pattern (often called a causal chain) links several events so that each effect becomes the cause of the next. Writers use chains to explain how a small starting event can lead to a large final result. Recognizing the chain helps you keep every link in order and spot a missing step, which is exactly what sequencing questions test. Look for chain markers such as 'this led to', 'which in turn', 'as a result', 'consequently' and 'this then caused'. For instance, a passage might explain that a factory closed, which in turn left hundreds of workers without jobs, which then reduced spending at local shops; each event is the effect of the one before it and the cause of the one after it.
log_node_12: Cascading cause-and-effect relationships (also known as multi-causal systems) involve several causes acting together, effects that branch in different directions, or loops where an effect strengthens its own cause. Academic writers use them to explain problems in climate, economics and health that no single cause can account for. Recognizing these patterns helps you avoid oversimplified answers and trace how a loop keeps a process going. Key markers include 'combined with', 'contributed to', 'triggered a cascade', 'in turn amplified' and 'a feedback loop', while hedges such as 'may contribute to' signal a weaker claim. For instance, when a passage says that warmer air dries the soil, dry soil heats the air further, and the hotter air dries the soil again, it describes a loop rather than a straight line.
log_node_13: A time-order sequence (also called process or step-by-step narration) lists the actions of a task in the exact order they must be done. Recipes, instructions and lab procedures depend on it, because doing a step too early can ruin the result. Recognizing this pattern helps you follow directions safely and spot when a step is out of place. Key signal words include 'first', 'before', 'next', 'while', 'once' and 'finally', and words like 'once' and 'until' tell you to wait for one step to finish before starting the next. For instance, a recipe that says 'First, boil the water; once it bubbles, add the pasta; finally, drain it' shows that adding the pasta depends on the water boiling, so the steps cannot be swapped.
snp_node_01: An addition transition (also called an additive connector) links two sentences that point in the same direction, so the second adds another idea of the same kind. Writers use these connectors to build a list of reasons, features or examples without making the reader guess how the ideas relate. Recognizing them helps you see that a passage is piling up support rather than changing its mind. Common addition connectors include 'and', 'also', 'in addition', 'besides' and 'too'. A useful test is to ask whether the second sentence gives one more of something. For instance, 'The library lends books. In addition, it offers free internet access' uses 'in addition' because the second sentence names another service, not a contrast or a result.
snp_node_02: Addition and sequence connectors (together called listing or enumerative transitions) both move a text forward, but they do different jobs. Addition connectors stack ideas of equal weight, while sequence connectors place steps or points in a set order. Writers often mix them in one paragraph, so you must notice whether the next sentence answers 'what else?' or 'what comes next?'. Recognizing the difference helps you choose the connector that keeps the passage coherent. Addition markers include 'moreover', 'furthermore' and 'as well', while sequence markers include 'first', 'second', 'then' and 'next'. For instance, 'First, preheat the oven. Next, grease the tray' calls for a sequence word because the steps follow in time, whereas 'The oven saves energy. Moreover, it runs quietly' needs an addition word.
snp_node_03: Advanced addition transitions (sometimes called emphatic or precision connectors) add a point while also showing how strong or how closely related it is. In academic writing, 'furthermore' and 'moreover' introduce a new supporting point, 'indeed' and 'in fact' strengthen the point just made, and 'similarly' adds a parallel case. Recognizing these shades of meaning helps you follow an argument's structure and avoid connectors that change what the writer claims. Cohesion also comes from repeated key terms and from phrases such as 'this' and 'these findings', which tie a new sentence back to the old one. For instance, 'The new timetable reduced delays. Indeed, trains now arrive on time almost every day' uses 'indeed' because the second sentence intensifies the first point instead of adding a separate benefit.
snp_node_04: A contrast transition (also called an adversative connector) signals that the next sentence turns against or differs from the one before it. Writers use contrast to show a surprise, a limitation or the other side of an idea. Recognizing it helps you notice when a passage changes direction, which often marks the writer's main point. Common contrast connectors include 'but', 'however', 'yet', 'on the other hand' and 'in contrast'. A quick test: if you can read the pair as this, but surprisingly that, you need a contrast word rather than an addition or result word. For instance, 'The forecast promised sunshine. However, heavy rain fell all afternoon' uses 'however' because the second sentence breaks the expectation set by the first.
snp_node_05: Intermediate contrast connectors (often split into contrast and concession transitions) separate two kinds of turn. A plain contrast places two different things side by side, while a concession admits that the first point is true but argues that something else still matters more. Writers use concession to sound fair while still making their case. Recognizing which kind of turn a sentence makes helps you choose a connector that keeps the logic exact. Contrast markers include 'on the other hand', 'whereas' and 'in contrast', while concession markers include 'nevertheless', 'even so', 'although' and 'still'. For instance, 'The hike was steep and tiring. Nevertheless, everyone reached the summit' uses 'nevertheless' because it accepts the difficulty and then shows the goal was reached anyway.
snp_node_06: Nuanced contrast (also known as corrective or qualifying contrast) appears in academic arguments when a writer does more than oppose two ideas. 'In contrast' compares two different subjects, 'however' turns against the previous claim, 'on the contrary' rejects a mistaken assumption after a negative statement, and 'admittedly' grants a point before answering it. Recognizing these differences helps you follow debates and avoid connectors that would reverse the writer's meaning. Cohesion devices such as 'this view' or 'such critics' also show exactly which earlier idea is being challenged. For instance, 'The study did not find the app harmful. On the contrary, users reported better sleep' uses 'on the contrary' because the second sentence pushes further in the same positive direction rather than disagreeing with the first.
snp_node_07: A cause-and-effect transition (also called a causal or result connector) shows that the second sentence happens because of the first. Writers use these connectors to explain consequences clearly, so readers do not have to guess how events are linked. Recognizing them helps you follow explanations in science, history and everyday instructions. Common result connectors include 'so', 'therefore', 'as a result', 'consequently' and 'thus'. Before choosing one, check the direction: the first sentence should describe the cause and the second its effect, never the other way around. For instance, 'The battery ran low. As a result, the phone switched off' uses 'as a result' because the low battery caused the phone to shut down, so the effect correctly follows its cause.
snp_node_08: Intermediate cause-and-effect connectors (often divided into result and reason transitions) point in opposite directions. Result connectors follow a cause and introduce its effect, while reason connectors follow an effect and introduce its cause. Writers use both, so you must check which sentence explains the other before choosing. Recognizing the direction helps you avoid a common trap where a connector sounds natural but reverses the logic. Result markers include 'consequently', 'as a result' and 'accordingly', while reason markers include 'this is because', 'the reason was that' and 'due to this'. Purpose markers such as 'so that' and 'in order to' describe a goal instead. For instance, 'The match was postponed. This is because the field had flooded' needs a reason connector, since the second sentence explains the first.
snp_node_09: Academic cause-and-effect transitions (also called causal and inferential connectors) separate real-world consequences from conclusions a writer reasons out. 'Consequently' and 'as a result' report something that happened because of an earlier event, while 'thus', 'hence' and 'it follows that' introduce a judgment drawn from evidence. Recognizing this difference helps you read research claims precisely and notice when a writer moves from facts to interpretation. Hedged links such as 'this may explain why' show a weaker, possible connection, and cohesion phrases like 'these results' or 'this trend' tie the conclusion back to its evidence. For instance, 'Only twelve people joined the trial. Hence, its findings cannot be applied to everyone' uses 'hence' because the second sentence is a conclusion the writer draws, not an event.
snp_node_10: A conclusion transition (also called a summarizing connector) signals that the writer is wrapping up and stating what the earlier points add up to. Writers place these connectors near the end of a paragraph or essay so readers know the main message is coming. Recognizing them helps you find the central idea quickly, which is useful for summary and main-idea questions. Common conclusion connectors include 'in conclusion', 'in short', 'to sum up', 'overall' and 'all in all'. The sentence after the connector should be broader than the details before it, not a new fact. For instance, 'Cycling is cheap, healthy and good for the air. In short, it is a smart way to travel' uses 'in short' because the last sentence sums up the three benefits.
snp_node_11: Intermediate conclusion connectors (often divided into summary and restatement transitions) end ideas in two different ways. A summary connector gathers several points into one judgment, while a restatement connector repeats the previous idea in simpler words without adding anything new. Writers use both to help readers hold onto key ideas. Recognizing which one a sentence needs helps you avoid choosing 'in conclusion' when the writer is only rephrasing. Summary markers include 'to conclude', 'on the whole' and 'in summary', while restatement markers include 'in other words', 'that is' and 'put simply'. For instance, 'The new law is revenue-neutral. In other words, it neither raises nor lowers taxes overall' uses a restatement connector because the second sentence explains the first in plainer language.
snp_node_12: Advanced conclusion signals (also called evaluative or weighing connectors) close an argument whose evidence points in more than one direction. 'All things considered' and 'on balance' show that the writer has weighed both sides, 'ultimately' names the final outcome after a process, and 'therefore' claims the evidence forces one result. Recognizing these differences helps you judge whether a conclusion is fair to the evidence or overstated. Cohesion devices such as 'these trade-offs' or 'despite these costs' link the verdict back to the mixed points before it. For instance, 'The stadium is costly and noisy, yet it brings tourists and jobs. On balance, the council decided to approve it' uses 'on balance' because the decision weighs real drawbacks against real benefits.
snp_node_13: Addition in a sequence (also called enumeration) lists several items or steps one after another, often with numbering words that keep them in order. Writers use it to present a set of reasons, tips or features so readers can count and remember them. Recognizing enumeration helps you see how many points a passage contains and where each new point begins. Common markers include 'first', 'second', 'also', 'another' and 'finally', and phrases like 'one more reason' signal a further item. For instance, 'There are three ways to save water. First, take shorter showers. Second, fix leaking taps. Finally, water plants in the evening' uses numbering words so each tip stands apart and the reader knows when the list is complete.
tap_node_01: A synonym clue (also called a restatement clue) is a familiar word placed near a difficult word that means almost the same thing. Writers add these clues so readers can understand a new word without stopping to look it up. Recognizing synonym clues helps you build vocabulary while you read and keeps the meaning of a passage clear. Look for the clue right beside the hard word, often after 'or', a comma, a dash, or the phrases 'also called' and 'that is'. You can test a clue by swapping it into the sentence in place of the hard word. For instance, in 'The puppy was lethargic, or sluggish and sleepy, after its long walk,' the words after 'or' show that lethargic means tired and lacking energy.
tap_node_02: Intermediate synonym clues (sometimes called scattered restatement) appear when a writer explains a difficult word with similar words that sit a little further away, often in the next clause or sentence. Writers use this to vary their language instead of repeating the same word. Recognizing it helps you connect words across a sentence and gather two clues instead of relying on one. Watch for linking signals such as a semicolon, a colon, 'similarly', 'just as' and 'likewise', and for pronouns like 'it' or 'this' that point back to the hard word. For instance, in 'The mayor's speech was succinct; it was short and to the point, lasting only two minutes,' the semicolon introduces 'short' and 'to the point', which together show that succinct means brief and clear.
tap_node_03: Advanced synonym clues (also called contextual restatement across clauses) require you to unlock more than one difficult word in the same passage, each explained by its own nearby synonyms. Academic writers often pack several demanding words into one sentence and restate each in plainer language. Recognizing which clue belongs to which word helps you avoid mixing up meanings. Split the sentence at signals such as 'while', 'whereas', semicolons and dashes, then match each hard word with the restatement inside its own section. For instance, in 'The first witness was garrulous, chatty and eager to talk, while the second was laconic, using as few words as possible,' the word 'while' divides the sentence, so garrulous means talkative and laconic means brief in speech.
tap_node_04: A definition clue (also called a direct explanation clue) is a phrase in the sentence that tells you exactly what a difficult word means. Textbooks and articles use these clues when they introduce a term the reader needs right away. Recognizing them helps you learn key vocabulary in science and social studies without reaching for a dictionary. Look for linking words such as 'is', 'means', 'refers to' and 'is called', or for an explanation set off by commas, dashes or parentheses right after the term. For instance, in 'Condensation, the process of water vapor turning into liquid, forms dew on the grass,' the words between the commas directly define condensation, so 'vapor' and 'liquid' are the key clue words to tap.
tap_node_05: Intermediate definition clues (sometimes called extended or two-part definitions) explain a word with more than one key idea, such as what something does and when or where it happens. Writers use these fuller explanations for words that a single synonym cannot capture. Recognizing that a definition has several parts helps you collect every important clue instead of stopping at the first one. Look for definition signals such as 'which means', 'is one that', 'is a kind of' and 'refers to', then pick out the content words that carry the meaning rather than the linking words. For instance, in 'A migratory bird is one that travels long distances each season to find food and warmth,' both 'travels' and 'season' are needed, because migratory means moving regularly with the seasons.
tap_node_06: Advanced definition clues (also called embedded academic definitions) appear when a passage defines two or more technical terms at once, each tucked into its own clause. Academic writers do this to keep explanations short, but it means each definition must be matched to the right term. Recognizing the boundaries of each definition helps you unlock both words accurately. Watch for definitions introduced by 'which is', 'known as', 'in other words' and paired commas or dashes, and remember that a definition almost always sits right after its own term. For instance, in 'The delta, a fan of soil deposited where a river meets the sea, is crossed by estuaries, which are wide river mouths where fresh and salt water mix,' each term is followed directly by its own definition.
tap_node_07: An antonym clue (also called a contrast clue) helps you understand a difficult word by placing it next to a word that means the opposite. Writers use contrast to make a meaning sharp and clear, especially when describing people, places or changes. Recognizing antonym clues lets you work out a word's meaning by flipping the meaning of the clue. Look for contrast signals such as 'unlike', 'but', 'however', 'instead of' and 'not', which tell you the nearby word is an opposite rather than a synonym. For instance, in 'Unlike her messy brother, Ana kept her room immaculate,' the word 'unlike' sets immaculate against 'messy', so immaculate must mean perfectly clean and tidy, the exact opposite of the brother's habits.
tap_node_08: Intermediate antonym clues (often called contrast clues across clauses) appear when the opposite word sits in a different part of the sentence, sometimes with more than one contrasting detail. Writers use 'rather than', 'whereas' and 'on the other hand' to set a difficult word against a fuller description of its opposite. Recognizing these clues helps you read the whole sentence, collect every contrasting detail and then reverse them. Common signals include 'rather than', 'whereas', 'instead', 'in contrast' and 'no longer'. For instance, in 'Rather than staying hostile, the two rival teams became friendly and helpful toward each other,' the clues 'friendly' and 'helpful' describe the opposite situation, which shows that hostile means unfriendly and aggressive.
tap_node_09: Advanced antonym clues (also called layered contrast clues) appear when one passage contains two or more difficult words, each explained by its own opposite. Academic and literary writers use paired contrasts to describe change, conflict or comparison in a compact way. Recognizing which contrast belongs to which word helps you avoid applying the wrong opposite. Look for several contrast signals in one sentence, such as 'unlike', 'not', 'while' and 'but', and treat each signal as the start of a separate clue zone. For instance, in 'The market was volatile last spring, unlike the steady, predictable prices of this year, and investors felt apprehensive, not confident,' 'unlike' pairs volatile with 'steady' and 'predictable', while 'not' pairs apprehensive with 'confident'.
tap_node_10: An example clue (also called an illustration clue) helps you understand a difficult word by giving familiar examples of it. Writers add examples when a definition alone would be too abstract for the reader. Recognizing example clues lets you work out a word's meaning by asking what the examples have in common. Look for signals such as 'such as', 'for example', 'for instance', 'including' and 'like', which introduce members of the group the hard word names. Once you find the examples, name the quality they all share. For instance, in 'The museum displays ancient artifacts, such as clay pots, stone tools and bronze coins,' every example is an object made and used by people long ago, so artifacts must mean human-made objects from the past.
tap_node_11: Intermediate example clues (sometimes called example-based inference) give two or more examples that you must compare to find the shared meaning of a difficult word. Writers often place these examples in the middle of a sentence, between commas or dashes, and add a describing detail at the end. Recognizing them helps you check your guess against every example and the extra detail, which makes your answer more reliable. Signals include 'for example', 'for instance', 'including', 'such as' and 'e.g.'. For instance, in 'Many crustaceans, for example crabs and lobsters, have hard shells and jointed legs,' the examples crabs and lobsters, together with the detail about shells and legs, show that crustaceans are hard-shelled water animals with jointed legs.
tap_node_12: Advanced inference clues (also called general-sense or logic clues) give no definition or example at all, so you must reason from causes, effects and descriptions around a difficult word. Writers rely on these clues in stories and articles that show rather than tell. Recognizing them helps you unlock hard words by asking what caused the situation, what it caused and what it looks like. Look for cause and effect signals such as 'after', 'because', 'so', 'which made' and 'as a result', and for vivid descriptive details. For instance, in 'After the long blackout, the town was desolate; empty streets, closed shops and silent houses stretched in every direction,' the cause and the empty, silent details together show that desolate means deserted and lifeless.
tap_node_13: A descriptive synonym clue (also called a description restatement) appears when a writer describes a person, place or thing and repeats the idea of a difficult word with simpler, similar words. Writers use this in stories and travel writing to keep descriptions vivid without confusing the reader. Recognizing it helps you notice that the easy words around a hard word are often just another way of saying it. Look for 'and', commas in a list of describing words, and phrases such as 'in other words' or 'that is'. For instance, in 'The old cabin was dilapidated, broken down and falling apart after years of storms,' the describing words 'broken down' and 'falling apart' restate dilapidated, so it means in very poor condition.
fac_node_01: Currency (also called timeliness) is the CRAAP criterion that asks whether information is recent enough for its topic. Writers and researchers must check currency because facts in fast-changing areas, such as technology, health and law, can become wrong within a few years. Recognizing outdated information helps you avoid repeating advice that no longer works. When checking currency, look for 'the publication date', words like 'currently', 'today' and 'the latest', and references to tools, prices or records that belong to an older time. Obviously outdated claims usually mention something almost nobody uses anymore. For instance, the statement 'the fastest way to send a document is by fax machine' fails currency, because email and messaging apps replaced fax machines for most people long ago.
fac_node_02: Intermediate currency checks (sometimes called date-to-topic matching) look for sources that are not ancient but are still too old for the claim they support. A ten-year-old source can be fine for history but misleading for social media trends, prices or medical guidance. Recognizing this helps you judge whether a date is acceptable for the specific topic instead of applying one rule to everything. Check whether 'latest', 'recent' or 'current' is attached to an old year, compare the source date with how fast the topic changes, and look for newer evidence that may have replaced it. For instance, the claim 'according to the latest 2012 survey, most teens send texts instead of using apps' fails currency, because messaging habits have changed several times since then.
fac_node_03: Advanced currency flaws (also called hidden staleness) occur when an outdated figure is presented as today's fact with no date at all, so the reader must know that the information has changed. Writers sometimes copy old numbers from earlier sources without updating them, and the claim still sounds precise. Recognizing hidden staleness helps you question undated statistics, records and rankings instead of trusting them because they look exact. Check phrases such as 'as of today', 'now' and 'currently', and compare any figure with benchmarks you know, such as population totals, world records or who holds an office. For instance, the statement 'Earth is currently home to about 6 billion people' fails currency, because world population passed 6 billion around 1999 and 8 billion in 2022.
fac_node_04: Relevance (also called topic fit) is the CRAAP criterion that asks whether a piece of information actually supports the topic and purpose of a text. Writers sometimes include sentences that are interesting or true but have nothing to do with the main point. Recognizing irrelevant information helps you focus on evidence that matters and spot padding in essays and articles. To check relevance, name the topic in a few words, then ask whether each sentence connects to 'the main idea', 'the question being answered' or 'the argument being made'. Completely off-topic sentences often sound like personal asides or random facts. For instance, in a report about recycling plastic, the sentence 'My favourite holiday destination is the beach' fails relevance, because it says nothing about recycling.
fac_node_05: Intermediate relevance checks (sometimes called keyword traps) look for sentences that share a word with the topic but do not support the actual point. A passage about the benefits of school gardens might mention gardens in a way that answers a completely different question. Recognizing this helps you judge sentences by their job in the argument, not by matching keywords. Ask whether the sentence 'supports the claim', 'answers the question' or 'adds evidence for the purpose', and be suspicious of history, trivia or definitions that drift from the main focus. For instance, in a passage arguing that school gardens improve students' diets, the sentence 'The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were one of the ancient wonders' fails relevance, even though it mentions gardens.
fac_node_06: Advanced relevance flaws (also called subtle scope drift) occur when a sentence stays in the same field and sounds scientific but shifts to a different population, time, place or question. Academic writers can drift without noticing, and the extra sentence looks like evidence even though it does not support the claim. Recognizing scope drift helps you check that evidence matches the exact claim being made. Compare the 'who', 'where' and 'when' of each sentence with the main claim, and watch for shifts from humans to animals, from children to adults, or from one country to another. For instance, in a passage about how screen time affects teenagers' sleep, a sentence reporting that adult office workers sleep less during busy seasons fails relevance, because it concerns a different group and cause.
fac_node_07: Authority (also called source credibility) is the CRAAP criterion that asks who created the information and whether they are qualified to make the claim. Writers support their points with sources, but a claim is only as strong as the person or organization behind it. Recognizing weak authority helps you avoid believing rumours and anonymous posts. To check authority, look for 'a named author', 'their qualifications', 'the organization they represent' and whether the source can be verified. Obviously unverified claims often come from 'someone online', 'an anonymous post' or 'people are saying'. For instance, the statement 'An anonymous account claims the city's tap water is unsafe to drink' fails authority, because nobody can check who wrote it or what they know about water safety.
fac_node_08: Intermediate authority checks (sometimes called expertise matching) look at sources that are named and even famous but are not qualified on the specific topic. Being well known, successful or popular does not make someone an expert in every field. Recognizing this helps you separate fame from real knowledge and give more weight to sources with relevant training or experience. Check whether the source's 'field of expertise' matches 'the topic of the claim', and whether the claim is backed by 'evidence' rather than reputation alone. For instance, the statement 'A famous football player says the new tax policy will ruin the economy' fails authority, because athletic success gives no special knowledge of economics, while an economist's analysis would carry far more weight.
fac_node_09: Advanced authority flaws (also called misplaced credentials) occur when a source has impressive qualifications, such as 'Dr.', 'professor' or 'award-winning', but the credentials belong to a different field from the claim. These titles can make a weak claim sound trustworthy, especially in academic writing. Recognizing misplaced credentials helps you read past the title to the actual area of expertise. Check 'the field of the degree or award', 'the institution', and whether the claim falls inside that field, and look for confirmation from experts who specialize in the topic. For instance, the statement 'Dr. Mara Velez, a prize-winning historian, says the new medicine cures migraines' fails authority, because a doctorate in history gives no expertise in medicine or drug testing.
fac_node_10: Accuracy (also called correctness and support) is the CRAAP criterion that asks whether information is true, supported by evidence and consistent with what is already well known. Writers can make mistakes, exaggerate or repeat myths, so a claim should never be accepted just because it is printed. Recognizing inaccurate information helps you avoid spreading false facts. To check accuracy, ask whether the claim is 'possible', whether it is 'supported by evidence' and whether it 'matches other reliable sources'. Wildly inaccurate claims break basic facts that most people learn in school. For instance, the statement 'The Sun travels around the Earth once every day' fails accuracy, because day and night come from the Earth's rotation, and it is the Earth that orbits the Sun, once a year.
fac_node_11: Intermediate accuracy checks (sometimes called fact verification) look for claims that keep the right subject but give a wrong detail, such as a date, distance or number that is far off. These errors are harder to spot than impossible claims because the sentence sounds reasonable. Recognizing them helps you compare details with facts you know and with other parts of the passage. Check 'numbers and units', 'dates and time periods' and 'names and places', and ask whether each figure fits your general knowledge. For instance, the statement 'The Pacific, the largest ocean on Earth, covers only about 2 percent of the planet's surface' fails accuracy, because the Pacific actually covers around 30 percent, so the figure is far too small for the largest ocean.
fac_node_12: Advanced accuracy flaws (also called fabricated or inconsistent statistics) occur when numbers look precise but contradict themselves or the rest of the passage. Writers who invent or misreport data often give exact-sounding percentages that cannot all be true together. Recognizing these flaws helps you test statistics instead of trusting them because they look scientific. Check whether 'percentages add up correctly', whether 'totals match their parts', and whether 'the sample size fits the claim', and be wary of 'studies show' with no named study. For instance, a survey of 300 students that reports 50 percent prefer art, 40 percent prefer music and 35 percent prefer drama, when each student chose only one subject, fails accuracy, because the shares add up to 125 percent.
fac_node_13: Purpose (also called intent) is the CRAAP criterion that asks why a piece of information was created: to inform, to persuade, to sell or to provoke. Writers with a hidden goal may use insults or emotional language instead of evidence. Recognizing purpose helps you tell a fair explanation from an attack or an advertisement. To check purpose, look for 'insults and name-calling', 'emotional or exaggerated words' and whether the text gives reasons or only opinions. Overtly biased language openly attacks people instead of discussing ideas. For instance, the statement 'Only fools would vote against the new park' fails purpose, because it insults anyone who disagrees rather than giving a single reason why the park is a good idea for the community.
fac_node_14: Intermediate purpose checks (sometimes called framing analysis) look for statements that report a real fact but wrap it in loaded words that tell the reader how to feel. Unlike open insults, biased framing can sound like normal reporting, so it is easier to miss. Recognizing it helps you separate the fact from the writer's judgment. Look for 'loaded adjectives' such as 'reckless', 'shameful' or 'heroic', 'one-sided word choices' and phrases like 'once again' that hint at a pattern without evidence. Try rewriting the sentence in neutral words to see what fact remains. For instance, 'The careless school board once again wasted money on new laptops' contains a fact, that laptops were bought, but 'careless' and 'wasted' are judgments that push the reader's opinion.
fac_node_15: Advanced purpose flaws (also called subtle persuasion or rhetorical manipulation) occur when a text sounds academic and calm but uses pressure phrases to shut down disagreement instead of presenting evidence. Writers may claim a consensus that does not exist or suggest that anyone who disagrees is unreasonable. Recognizing these techniques helps you notice when a scholarly tone is hiding a persuasive goal. Watch for 'appeals to consensus' such as 'as every expert agrees', 'loaded presuppositions' such as 'obviously' and 'clearly', and phrases that dismiss critics without answering them. For instance, the sentence 'Any serious scientist now accepts that the program works, so its critics simply misunderstand the data' fails purpose, because it replaces evidence with social pressure and labels critics instead of answering them.
fac_node_16: Currency in technology guides (also called version timeliness) asks whether instructions still match the tools people use today. Technology changes so fast that a guide written a decade ago may describe software, devices or steps that no longer exist. Recognizing outdated technology advice helps you avoid wasting time on steps that cannot work. When checking a guide, look for 'old device names', 'discontinued software or services', 'old version numbers' and 'the date of the guide'. If a step depends on something most people can no longer buy or install, the guide fails currency. For instance, an instruction saying 'Save your homework onto a floppy disk before taking it to school' fails currency, because floppy disks and their drives disappeared from ordinary computers many years ago.
